title: ASU Health Observatory releases family heat response plan for summer safety
text:
ASU Health Observatory releases family heat response plan for summer safety
Arizona State University's Health Observatory has introduced a Family Heat Response Plan to help residents prepare for potential power outages during extreme summer heat, according to a July 13 announcement. The initiative aims to guide families in planning where they will go, how they will care for pets, and which neighbors they may need to check on if air conditioning fails.
“We’re treating it as the disaster it is,” said Meaghan Batchelor, an epidemiologist and principal population health data scientist at the Health Observatory. Batchelor developed the questionnaire that prompts users to consider practical steps such as pet arrangements and neighbor welfare. “I grew up in Arizona and I remember practicing fire drills but we never practiced what would happen if the power went out,” she said.
The Health Observatory was launched in 2024 as an early warning system for public health using data analysis. Its website now offers interactive resources on heat-related illness prevention, including a quiz and frequently asked questions section about living with extreme heat. It also provides links to state and national resources for outdoor workers and templates for workplace heat illness prevention programs.
Rebecca Sunenshine, medical director of the ASU Health Observatory, said that anyone struggling financially could be at risk of heat-related illness due to high utility bills leading some people not to use air conditioning sufficiently. “Because our utility bills are so expensive in the summer in Arizona, people will not turn on their air conditioning or they won't turn it on high enough,” Sunenshine said. She added that cooling centers are essential resources: “You cannot spend the night in an un-air conditioned environment during the summer here when there's a power outage.”
Sunenshine referenced research by Jennifer Vanos from ASU’s School of Sustainability indicating that individuals need at least 70 minutes inside a cooling center to reach safe body temperatures. “When we get scientific information like that, it can really change prevention across Arizona and the United States,” Sunenshine said.
The School of Sustainability at Arizona State University advances research and education promoting environmental integrity, social equity—including highlighting Indigenous sciences—and well-being; supports student research through grants; utilizes facilities such as Wrigley Hall with graduate workspaces; functions within ASU's Rob Walton College of Global Futures; and its graduates have served on various environmental bodies, according to the official website.
